title: North-Bound Distribution of Link-State and Traffic Engineering Information Using BGP
summary: Systems outside a network sometimes need its topology and traffic engineering information, normally carried by IGPs. This standards-track RFC defines a way to carry that link-state information in BGP, so external components such as path computation elements can collect it. It was replaced by RFC 9552.

eli5.summary: A map-making robot outside a city needs to know the roads. This lets routers tell it by using a message system they already have.

questions: how to export igp topology via bgp
how does bgp carry link-state information
subtitle: How routers hand their network map to outside tools by carrying link-state data inside BGP.

tldr.problem: Path computation elements and ALTO servers sit outside the network but need its topology and traffic engineering data, which normally stays inside the IGP's link-state database.
tldr.mechanism: A new BGP NLRI format (AFI 16388, SAFI 71 or 72) describes nodes, links and prefixes, and a new BGP-LS attribute carries their properties, so BGP can export the IGP view in an IGP-neutral way.
tldr.outcome: BGP-LS gives external consumers one interface for topology data, under operator policy. This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 9552.

today: RFC 7752 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9552, which is now the place to look for the current BGP-LS specification. It was also updated by RFC 9029.

sections.title: Why and How: Link-State Data in BGP
sections.content:
An IGP's link-state database (LSDB) or traffic engineering database (TED) only describes one IGP area. Applications such as end-to-end traffic engineering would benefit from seeing beyond one area or autonomous system.

The RFC names two consumers. A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths across several areas or ASes and needs the TED. Many implementations make the PCE a passive IGP participant, which the RFC says may be sub-optimal under high churn or when one PCE serves many areas. An ALTO server builds an abstracted network topology for applications such as peer-to-peer clients or CDNs, and needs both prefix data (from BGP) and TE data (from an IGP).

BGP-LS gives both of them a single interface to the network.

The specification has two parts: a new Link-State NLRI that names nodes, links and prefixes, and a new BGP-LS attribute that carries their properties, such as link metrics. The RFC aims to keep content IGP-neutral so that a consumer does not need to know OSPF or IS-IS specifics.

The NLRI is carried in MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI. Non-VPN data uses AFI 16388 / SAFI 71 and VPN data uses AFI 16388 / SAFI 72. Two speakers MUST use BGP capability advertisement to confirm both can process it.

A BGP speaker applies configurable policy. It may export the real physical topology, or an abstracted one in which virtual aggregated nodes are joined by virtual paths. Making such abstractions is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5:
Some helpers outside the network, like a route planner, need to know the whole map. Listening to every road crew separately is messy, so the routers pass the map along in one familiar way.

The routers write down places and roads in a special notebook format. Both sides first check that they can read that notebook before they swap.

sections.title: NLRI Types and TLV Encoding
sections.content:
Everything is encoded as Type/Length/Value (TLV) triplets with 16-bit Type and Length fields. Unrecognized types MUST be preserved and propagated, and TLVs MUST be sorted by type so that NLRIs with unknown TLVs can still be compared.

There are four NLRI types: Node (1), Link (2), IPv4 Topology Prefix (3) and IPv6 Topology Prefix (4). Each starts with a one-octet Protocol-ID naming the source (IS-IS Level 1 or 2, OSPFv2, Direct, Static configuration, OSPFv3) and a 64-bit Identifier naming the routing universe. Well-known value 0 means the default Layer 3 routing topology.

A Link NLRI describes a unidirectional half-link, so a point-to-point link needs two Link NLRIs, one from each end. The 'Direct' and 'Static configuration' protocol IDs are for locally sourced or virtual information.
sections.eli5: Every note says who wrote it and which map it belongs to. A road between two towns is written down twice, once from each town.

sections.title: Identifying Nodes, Links and Prefixes
sections.content:
Node Descriptors anchor each link. The Local Node Descriptors TLV is mandatory in all NLRI types and the Remote Node Descriptors TLV is mandatory for Link NLRIs. They contain sub-TLVs: Autonomous System (512), BGP-LS Identifier (513), OSPF Area-ID (514) and the mandatory IGP Router-ID (515).

The goal is that the same node is never represented by two keys and two different nodes never share a key. The AS number and BGP-LS Identifier together MUST be globally unique, which disambiguates IGP router IDs that are private or have no global registry.

Link Descriptors tell parallel links apart using interface and neighbor addresses, or link local/remote identifiers when addresses are absent. Prefix Descriptors carry the IP reachability prefix, an optional OSPF route type and an optional Multi-Topology ID.
sections.eli5: To avoid mixing up two towns with the same name, each address also includes the country and region it belongs to.

sections.title: The BGP-LS Attribute
sections.content:
The BGP-LS attribute is an optional, non-transitive BGP attribute built from TLVs. It SHOULD only be included with Link-State NLRIs and MUST be ignored for other address families.

Node attribute TLVs include node flag bits (such as the overload bit), a node name, IS-IS area identifiers and router IDs. Link attribute TLVs reuse the format of IS-IS extended reachability sub-TLVs and may carry data sourced from either IS-IS or OSPF. Prefix attribute TLVs describe the advertised prefixes.

An opaque attribute TLV lets a router pass along native protocol data that has no protocol-neutral form yet, bridging the lag between a new IGP feature and its BGP-LS definition.
sections.eli5: The notebook has a second page for extra details about each town and road, like how wide or busy it is.

sections.title: Aggregation and Inter-AS Links
sections.content:
Distributing every link in the global Internet is not desirable from a scaling and privacy point of view, so an implementation may support link to path aggregation. An ASBR can advertise an aggregate link between a non-adjacent pair of nodes instead of its real links. Whether to expose all links or aggregates is an operator policy choice.

The RFC walks through three examples: no aggregation, ASBR to ASBR aggregation, and multi-AS aggregation where a whole AS is modeled as one node. The IGP is not active on inter-AS links, so an implementation SHOULD provide some way to inject them into BGP-LS.
sections.eli5: A neighbor can show you the real streets in their town, or just one big road marked on your map that hides the details.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions do not change the BGP security model. A speaker MUST NOT accept updates from a consumer peer, which can be enforced by manually configuring consumer peers. Operators SHOULD protect against DDoS from consumers, for example by rate-limiting multiple session attempts.

Exporting topology is also a confidentiality risk for sensitive network information. Because BGP peerings are not automatic, the operator is responsible for configuring only trusted consumers.
sections.eli5: Only people you trust should get your map, and they may read it but never scribble on it.
